claims.statement: mc-service converts every DomainError into an RFC 9457 Problem Details response: domain_error_to_response() maps each variant through the shared problem_response() helper, which serves application/problem+json with type, title, status and detail members, as the constitution's error-handling rule requires for HTTP APIs.

problem_response() builds the RFC 9457 type member as https://mc-service.example/errors/{ERROR_CODE} — a deliberately non-resolvable namespace under the RFC 2606 reserved .example TLD, not the deployment domain, so assertions match the URI suffix rather than rewriting it to a real host.

domain_error_to_response() exhaustively matches every DomainError variant, so adding a domain error without a response arm is a compile error and there is no fallback path that could serialize a panic or Rust backtrace; DomainError::Internal(msg) logs the internal message server-side via tracing::error! but returns the generic 'An unexpected error occurred. Please try again later.' detail.

DomainError::ValidationError(msg) is the one variant that echoes a constructed message across the response boundary: it becomes a 400 INVALID_INPUT whose detail is msg verbatim, so any new ValidationError message is client-visible. Existing producers keep it safe with fixed sentences such as 'Invalid pagination cursor' in the keyset decoder and 'Search text is not a valid pattern' when search text cannot be escaped into a BSON regex.

The error-code string in the type URI (COLLECTION_NOT_FOUND, MOVIE_NOT_FOUND, DUPLICATE_COLLECTION_NAME, DUPLICATE_MOVIE, INVALID_INPUT, OWNED_MEDIA_WHEN_NOT_OWNED, RIP_QUALITY_WHEN_NOT_RIPPED, ACCESS_DENIED, INTERNAL_ERROR) is the stable machine-readable identifier, and it is not derived from the Rust variant name — DomainError::ValidationError maps to INVALID_INPUT — so expected codes cannot be generated by naming the enum variant.

A 404 from mc-service is a refusal as often as an absence: COLLECTION_NOT_FOUND and MOVIE_NOT_FOUND are returned for cross-tenant access as well as for genuinely missing records and are deliberately indistinguishable. authorize_collection_access() documents the rule, and the repository's ownerId/collectionId-scoped filters produce the same error for a foreign-owned document. The OpenAPI NotFound description states it, and the integration tests assert the refusal is never a 403 and that the foreign document is still present and unmodified.

The 'every error is application/problem+json' rule holds only for DomainError paths. require_app_role in api/middleware/auth.rs returns axum::Json directly as its error type, so its 403 is served as application/json with type https://httpstatuses.io/403 rather than the mc-service.example namespace, and the 401 comes from KeycloakAuthLayer rather than problem_response(). Feature 046 records aligning the middleware with problem_response as the prerequisite for testing that 403.

DomainError::AccessDenied, the only variant that would produce a 403 ACCESS_DENIED problem document, has no production producer in mc-service; it appears only in mocked unit tests, so a 403 observed in practice comes from require_app_role.

The problem body's member order is part of the bytes on the wire, so mc-service must keep serde_json = { features = ["preserve_order"] } named explicitly in Cargo.toml. bson 2 enabled that feature implicitly and bson 3 does not, so during the bson 2 to 3 upgrade the feature was lost with all tests green and every json! object — including the problem body — silently reordered to alphabetical; the order is now pinned by problem_body_keeps_rfc_9457_member_order_on_the_wire in error_handler.rs.

The OpenAPI ProblemDetail schema in api-specs/mc-service-api.yaml declares an optional instance member, but problem_response() emits only type, title, status and detail, so no mc-service response ever carries instance — reading the schema alone would wrongly suggest a correlation identifier is available in the body.

The BFF loses the problem media type on every RFC 9457-shaped path except the account-deletion routes. handleMcApiError() in mc-api-error.ts propagates an upstream mc-service body and status verbatim through Response.json(err.response.data, ...), and securityHeaders() sets only CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy and never a Content-Type, so a proxied mc-service failure reaches the client as application/json while still carrying the mc-service.example type URI. Only problemResponse() in account-route-support.ts sets Content-Type: application/problem+json explicitly. Every other about:blank problem document is served as application/json: problem() and its notFound() wrapper in backup-route-support.ts — the single refusal helper for all /bff-api/backups/* routes, covering the validation 400s, the 404 that means 'not yours' as well as 'not there', the 409 for a destination with no stored credential, the 422 for a failed artifact verification and the 502 for a refused consent revocation — plus the inline literals in the agent-config, agent-config-test and backups-tick routes. That makes the gap the normal case rather than a corner: a problem-media-type assertion holds only against mc-service directly or on the account-deletion routes, and fails on any backups route. The two helpers otherwise agree on the shape, which is what lets a client parse both: type, title and status are always present, detail is added only when supplied rather than emitted as null, and the body's status equals the HTTP status line. Closing the media-type gap needs no new plumbing — securityHeaders() takes an optional HeadersInit and copies it before stamping the baseline headers. A client must therefore expect both the mc-service.example namespace and about:blank, and about:blank means 'no more specific type than the status code' by RFC 9457, not an unknown service.

mc-service's shared auth layer answers every credential it cannot decode or validate with 401 and the library's generic {"error":"invalid_token"} body; a request with no credential is also 401, so only the body — not the status — distinguishes a malformed token from a missing one. movie_metadata_rejects_a_malformed_token asserts exactly that pair (401 plus the invalid_token body), which is what proves the layer actually tried to decode the credential rather than merely checking the header was present.

handleMcApiError()'s AuthError branch and its unexpected-error fallback do not answer with an RFC 9457 document: they return Response.json({ error, code }, ...) as application/json, so a BFF-originated auth or 500 refusal carries neither type, title nor detail, unlike the axios branch which forwards a problem-shaped upstream body. The AuthError branch additionally attaches whatever the error itself carries — one Set-Cookie line per AuthError.clearCookies entry and a Retry-After on a retryable 503 — through the shared authErrorHeaders() helper.

The BFF's own published API contracts declare application/problem+json for error responses their implementations serve as application/json: the backups contract (specs/073-scheduled-backups/contracts/bff-backups-api.yaml) declares it for the destination-creation 400 and the restore 422, and the movies-count contract documents '4xx application/problem+json (via handleMcApiError)', while problem() in backup-route-support.ts and handleMcApiError()'s proxy branch both use Response.json(). The account-deletion contract (specs/076-account-deletion/contracts/bff-api.md) drifts the other way: it attributes its errors to backup-route-support's problem() — the helper that does not serve the problem media type — while the routes actually import problemResponse() from account-route-support.ts, which does. The declared body shape is correct — the backups Problem schema is type/title/status/detail and never an upstream body — so a generated client parses the bodies but a Content-Type assertion derived from the contract fails.

The BFF client's generic getErrorMessage() in src/utils/errors.ts understands only an auth-vocabulary body with a `code` member, so an RFC 9457 refusal that carries title/detail instead collapses to the generic 'An unexpected error occurred. Please try again.' Several call sites therefore read the problem members directly: extractErrorMessage() in src/hooks/use-movies.ts (detail, then title, then message) and backupErrorMessage() in src/hooks/backup-error-message.ts (detail then title, falling back to getErrorMessage), plus the upload catch in src/hooks/use-spreadsheet-import.ts (detail), failureReason() in src/bff-server/backup-restore-writer.ts (title, then 'mc-service answered HTTP {status}') and test() in src/hooks/use-assistant-config.tsx (title). backupErrorMessage's comment records the general gap as a separate item rather than widening the shared auth error mapper.

The BFF answers errors in two incompatible client vocabularies. The auth and admin routes (auth/login, auth/refresh, auth/logout, auth/user, auth/register, auth/resend-verification, auth/verify-email, admin/settings) return { error, code } with no type, title or detail — the same vocabulary as handleMcApiError()'s AuthError and unexpected-error branches; auth/register funnels every branch through its local extractError() and re-maps the code to a user-facing sentence in getUserMessage() rather than exposing anything upstream. The proxy and backups routes instead return RFC 9457-shaped bodies. The shared getErrorMessage() in src/utils/errors.ts is built for the first dialect only: it extracts a code member and maps it through AUTH_ERROR_MESSAGES, so a problem-shaped body with no code collapses to the generic 'An unexpected error occurred. Please try again.'

The 401-instead-of-400 answer for an unparseable credential is a dependency behaviour that changed in axum-keycloak-auth 0.8.4: 0.8.3 returned 400 with the parse error in the body, and 0.8.4 replaced it with the generic 401 invalid_token response as a security fix. mc-service stays on that line — the manifest asks for 0.8 and spec 091's FR-003 forbids pinning back — and spec 091 records that the old 400 assertion in movie_metadata_rejects_a_malformed_token was the only thing that broke (every other auth assertion already expected 401 or 403) with no production code change. Because api/middleware/logging.rs emits an auth_failure audit event on any 401, malformed tokens are now recorded where the old 400 was not.

mc-service installs no axum rejection mapper, so a request the framework's own extractors cannot deserialize never reaches problem_response(): a JSON body of the wrong shape (a missing required field or a wrong type) is answered with axum's own 422, a syntactically invalid body with its 400, a missing or wrong Content-Type with its 415, and query parameters that fail to deserialize with its 400 — bodies carrying neither the mc-service.example type namespace nor the type/title/detail members. api-specs/mc-service-api.yaml declares application/problem+json for BadRequest, Unauthorized, Forbidden, NotFound and Conflict and declares no 422 at all, so that path has no contract schema, and no test in the suite exercises it (the 400 INVALID_INPUT assertions call the command handlers directly rather than over HTTP). The 422 is corroborated from the other side by docs/runbooks/agent-layer.md, which records that the agent's movie payload sends `rated` as a present key precisely because CreateMovieDto 422s an omission.
